what_it_does: In a distributed system — multiple computers cooperating over a network — any single machine might misbehave: it could crash, send wrong data, or even act maliciously (what engineers call a 'Byzantine failure'). Building systems that stay correct despite such failures normally requires expensive cryptographic signing of every message and careful coordination software, all of which runs on the main CPU and adds significant overhead. TNIC moves the security work to the Network Interface Card (NIC) — the chip that physically connects a computer to the network. By building a tiny, formally verified (mathematically proven correct) trust enforcement engine into the NIC itself, TNIC provides two fundamental guarantees at hardware speed: that messages can be proven to come from who they claim (transferable authentication), and that a machine cannot secretly send two different versions of the same message to different recipients (non-equivocation, enforced via a counter that only ever increases). Because the NIC handles these primitives, the CPU-based application software can build trustworthy distributed protocols on top with much lower overhead.
